title: NAT Traversal for AI Agents: A Deep Dive
description: How Pilot Protocol gets agents talking behind NAT: STUN discovery, UDP hole-punching, and automatic relay fallback. See the technical details.
seoTitle: NAT Traversal for AI Agents: A Deep Dive | Pilot Protocol
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: NAT is the single biggest obstacle to peer-to-peer communication on the modern internet.

sit behind some form of Network Address Translation. They can make outbound connections, but they cannot receive inbound ones. For AI agents that need to collaborate, coordinate, and exchange data in real time, this is not an inconvenience -- it is a showstopper.

Pilot Protocol handles this with a layered NAT traversal strategy that runs automatically. The agent developer never writes traversal code, never configures port forwarding, and never sets up a VPN. This article goes deep into the mechanics: what NAT does to UDP packets, how the four NAT types differ, how STUN discovery works, how beacon-coordinated hole-punching opens paths through restrictive NATs, and how relay fallback keeps agents connected behind symmetric NATs and carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT), as long as both can reach the beacon.
If you want the high-level overview first, see
Connect AI Agents Behind NAT -- Without a VPN
. This post is the deep dive.

introduced Network Address Translation in 1994 as a stopgap for IPv4 address exhaustion (RFC 3022 later obsoleted it in 2001). A NAT device maps multiple private addresses (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) to a single public IP, rewriting packet headers on the fly. Outbound traffic works because the NAT records each mapping and routes responses back to the correct internal host.

Inbound traffic is the problem. When Agent A behind NAT-1 wants to send a UDP packet to Agent B behind NAT-2, it addresses the packet to NAT-2's public IP. NAT-2 receives the packet, looks up its mapping table for a matching entry, finds none -- because Agent B never sent a packet to Agent A's NAT -- and drops it silently. The packet vanishes without a trace.
This is not a bug. This is the entire point of NAT: unsolicited inbound traffic is rejected. It is an accidental firewall, and it blocks every peer-to-peer protocol that does not account for it.

fields.code:
# What happens when two agents behind NAT try to talk directly

Agent A (192.168.1.50)        NAT-1 (203.0.113.10)        NAT-2 (198.51.100.20)        Agent B (10.0.0.42)
       |                            |                            |                            |
       |--- UDP to 198.51.100.20 -->|--- UDP to 198.51.100.20 -->|                            |
       |                            |                            |--- DROP (no mapping) ---X  |
       |                            |                            |                            |
       |                            |                            |<-- UDP to 203.0.113.10 ----|
       |                            |--- DROP (no mapping) ---X  |                            |
       |                            |                            |                            |
# Both packets are dropped. Neither NAT has a mapping for the other.

children.text: For AI agents, this means that two agents running on developer laptops, inside Docker containers, on edge devices, or behind corporate firewalls cannot communicate directly. Every agent-to-agent framework that assumes reachable endpoints -- Google's A2A, HTTP-based MCP servers, REST APIs -- fails silently when NAT is involved.
The Four NAT Types: From Friendly to Hostile
Not all NATs behave the same way.
classifies NAT behavior into four types based on how they create and enforce address/port mappings. Understanding these types is essential because each one requires a different traversal strategy.
The friendliest NAT type. Once an internal host sends a packet to any external address, the NAT creates a mapping and allows
to send packets back through that mapping.
STUN discovery is sufficient. Learn the public endpoint, register it, and accept direct connections from any peer. No hole-punching needed.
The NAT only forwards inbound packets from IP addresses that the internal host has previously sent packets to. The port does not matter -- any port from a known IP is allowed.

fields.code:
# Restricted Cone NAT behavior
Internal sends to 198.51.100.5:9000
NAT maps to 203.0.113.10:54321

# Only 198.51.100.5 can send back (any port)
198.51.100.5:9000  --->  203.0.113.10:54321  ✓  (same IP, same port)
198.51.100.5:8888  --->  203.0.113.10:54321  ✓  (same IP, different port)
10.20.30.40:9000   --->  203.0.113.10:54321  ✗  (different IP -- DROPPED)

children.text: Hole-punching. Both agents must send a packet to each other first, so each NAT adds the other's IP to its allowed list. The beacon coordinates the simultaneous send.
The strictest cone variant. The NAT only forwards packets from the
that the internal host sent to. This is a common NAT type in enterprise and residential environments.
Hole-punching, same as Restricted Cone. The agents must send to each other's exact public endpoint. The beacon coordinates timing so the holes overlap.
The most hostile type. The NAT creates a
different external port for each destination
. The port discovered via STUN (talking to the beacon) is not the same port assigned when talking to a peer. Hole-punching fails because neither side knows the other's actual port.

fields.code:
# Symmetric NAT behavior
Internal sends to beacon   198.51.100.1:9001  --->  NAT maps to 203.0.113.10:54321
Internal sends to peer     10.20.30.40:4000   --->  NAT maps to 203.0.113.10:54322  (DIFFERENT port!)

# Peer tries STUN-discovered port 54321 -- FAILS
10.20.30.40:4000  --->  203.0.113.10:54321  ✗  (wrong mapping)

# The correct port is 54322, but the peer has no way to know this

children.text: Relay through the beacon. Direct connection and hole-punching are both impossible because the port is unpredictable. The beacon forwards encrypted packets between the two agents.

The practical takeaway: the three cone types allow direct peer-to-peer connections through STUN discovery and hole-punching. Symmetric NATs (and carrier-grade NATs that behave like them) require relay. A complete solution must handle all four types without manual configuration.
STUN Discovery: Learning Your Public Endpoint
The first step in NAT traversal is self-discovery. An agent behind NAT does not know its own public IP address or the external port assigned by the NAT.
STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT, RFC 5389)
solves this by reflecting the observed source address back to the sender.

server provides the STUN function. When a daemon starts, it sends a STUN-like UDP probe to the beacon on a temporary socket. The beacon reads the source IP and port from the UDP header -- which is the NAT-mapped public endpoint -- and sends it back as the response payload.

STUN discovery uses a temporary UDP socket that is closed before the tunnel binds the same port. This is critical -- if both the STUN response listener and the tunnel read loop compete for the same socket, a race condition causes dropped packets. The sequence is: open temporary socket, send STUN probe, receive response, close socket, then start the tunnel on the same port.
After STUN discovery, the daemon registers its public endpoint with the rendezvous server. Other agents can now look up this endpoint and attempt connections.

fields.code:
# Start the daemon; discovery and registration happen in the background
$ pilotctl daemon start --email agent@example.com
Daemon running (pid 48211)
  Address:  0:0000.0000.0005
  Hostname: data-processor
  Socket:   /tmp/pilot.sock
  Logs:     /home/agent/.pilot/pilot-48211.log

children.text: For agents running on cloud VMs with stable public IPs, STUN discovery is unnecessary. The
flag lets operators specify the public endpoint directly, skipping STUN entirely:

fields.code:
# Cloud VM with known public IP -- skip STUN
$ pilotctl daemon start --email agent@example.com --listen :4000 --endpoint 203.0.113.10:4000

children.text: For Restricted Cone and Port-Restricted Cone NATs, STUN discovery reveals the public endpoint but does not make it reachable. The NAT drops inbound packets from unknown sources. Hole-punching solves this by making both NATs think the other agent is a known source.

The technique is simple in concept: both agents send a UDP packet to each other at the same time. Each outbound packet creates a mapping in the sender's NAT that allows the other agent's packets through. The trick is timing -- both sides must send before either NAT's mapping expires.
Pilot Protocol's beacon coordinates this timing with two message types:
-- sent by the initiating agent to the beacon, naming the target agent by node ID
-- sent by the beacon to both agents simultaneously, containing each other's public endpoint

fields.code:
# Hole-punch coordination via beacon

Agent A                      Beacon                      Agent B
(port_restricted)                                    (restricted_cone)
   |                           |                           |
   |-- MsgPunchRequest(B) ---->|                           |
   |                           |-- MsgPunchCommand(A) ---->|
   |<-- MsgPunchCommand(B) ----|                           |
   |                           |                           |
   |                        [~same instant]                |
   |==== UDP to B's endpoint =============================>|  creates mapping on A's NAT
   |<============================= UDP to A's endpoint ====|  creates mapping on B's NAT
   |                           |                           |
   |<============== direct traffic ========================>|
   |                     (NATs have mappings,               |
   |                      beacon not involved)              |

# After hole-punch succeeds, traffic is purely peer-to-peer.
# The beacon is no longer in the data path.

children.text: The beacon sends the two MsgPunchCommand messages back to back while it handles the request, so both sides start punching at nearly the same time. Both NATs create mappings, and subsequent packets from either side pass through the newly opened holes.
After hole-punching succeeds, the connection is
. Latency is peer-to-peer with no relay overhead. Throughput is limited only by the underlying network. The beacon is completely out of the loop.

NAT mappings have a timeout, typically 30-120 seconds for UDP. The hole-punch works because both outbound packets create mappings before either mapping expires. If one side sends significantly before the other, its packet arrives at the remote NAT before the remote NAT has a mapping for it, and gets dropped. The beacon's coordinated send keeps the timing window tight.
Pilot retries the connection if the first attempt fails. The retry ladder is built into the DialConnection function (direct attempts, then relay) -- the agent developer never sees it.
Relay Fallback: Connectivity for Symmetric NAT

Symmetric NATs defeat hole-punching because the external port changes with each destination. When Agent A sends a STUN probe to the beacon, the NAT assigns port 54321. When Agent A sends a hole-punch packet to Agent B, the NAT assigns port 54322. Agent B is aiming for port 54321. The packets miss each other.
There is no algorithmic solution to this. Port prediction techniques exist but are unreliable and vendor-specific. The only reliable approach is
: route traffic through a third party that both agents can reach.
In Pilot Protocol, the beacon doubles as a relay server. When hole-punching fails, the daemon automatically switches to relay mode using the

fields.code:
# MsgRelay wire format
Byte 0:      0x05           # Message type: MsgRelay
Bytes 1-4:   senderNodeID   # 4-byte node ID of the sender
Bytes 5-8:   destNodeID     # 4-byte node ID of the destination
Bytes 9+:    payload        # Encrypted tunnel frame (PILS)

# The beacon reads destNodeID, looks up the destination's
# UDP address, and forwards the payload.

children.text: A critical security property: the relay payload is

. The tunnel between Agent A and Agent B uses X25519 key exchange and AES-256-GCM encryption. The beacon sees only the MsgRelay header (sender and destination node IDs) and opaque encrypted bytes. It cannot read, modify, or forge the content. A compromised beacon could drop traffic and see which nodes talk to each other, but it could not read what they say.
For details on the encryption layer, see
Automatic NAT Detection and Strategy Selection

Pilot's DialConnection function implements the complete traversal logic as a state machine. No configuration is needed. The daemon uses STUN to discover its public endpoint, then applies a fixed direct→relay fallback ladder — it does not classify the NAT type; symmetric-NAT peers are simply relayed after a direct dial fails.

fields.code:
# DialConnection retry logic (simplified)

1. Look up target's endpoint from rendezvous server
2. Phase 1 — Direct: DialDirectRetries (3) attempts with exponential
   backoff (initial RTO 250ms, capped at 8s)
   - If the direct path works: use it
   - If all direct attempts fail: continue to Phase 2
3. Phase 2 — Relay: remaining attempts (DialMaxRetries total = 7, i.e. 4
   relay attempts) wrap traffic through the beacon
   - Works as long as both agents can reach the beacon

# Two phases, 7 total attempts (3 direct + 4 relay)

children.text: The application layer receives a standard
interface regardless of which tier succeeded. The connection object supports Read, Write, Close, SetDeadline, and all other methods. Standard Go HTTP servers, gRPC clients, and any protocol built on
work transparently over any traversal tier.

The daemon does not detect or classify the NAT type, and it does not need to. STUN tells it its public endpoint; the fixed direct-then-relay ladder then reaches any peer that can reach the beacon, whatever kind of NAT sits in between. If you want to know which path a peer ended up on,
shows it in the PATH column (
Here is the complete sequence for connecting two agents behind different NAT types on different networks.

fields.code:
# Agent A: behind Port-Restricted Cone NAT on a home network
$ pilotctl init --registry 34.71.57.205:9000 --hostname research-agent
$ pilotctl daemon start --email research@example.com
Daemon running (pid 48211)
  Address:  0:0000.0000.000A
  Hostname: research-agent
  Socket:   /tmp/pilot.sock
  Logs:     /home/research/.pilot/pilot-48211.log

# Agent B: behind Symmetric NAT on a corporate network
$ pilotctl init --hostname data-warehouse
$ pilotctl daemon start --email warehouse@example.com
Daemon running (pid 3170)
  Address:  0:0000.0000.000B
  Hostname: data-warehouse
  Socket:   /tmp/pilot.sock
  Logs:     /home/warehouse/.pilot/pilot-3170.log

# Establish mutual trust (required before connection)
# On Agent A, using B's node ID (a private node's hostname only resolves for peers that already trust it):
$ pilotctl handshake 11 "Need access to training dataset"
handshake request sent to node 11
  they must approve on their side · check status: pilotctl trust · propagation can take ~60s

# On Agent B:
$ pilotctl pending
$ pilotctl approve 10
trust established with node 10
  trust is now mutual — message them: pilotctl send-message 10 --data "hi"

# On Agent A: connect to Agent B
$ pilotctl ping data-warehouse --count 4
PING 0:0000.0000.000B
# one line per reply: seq=N bytes=N time=<RTT>  [dial=<time> echo=<time>]

# Which path did it take? The PATH column shows relay for this peer
$ pilotctl peers --all

children.text: Agent B is behind symmetric NAT, so direct connection and hole-punching both fail. The daemon automatically falls back to relay. The developer's command is simply
-- the seven dial attempts (three direct, four relayed) and the switch to relay happen inside DialConnection.
Now consider a scenario where both agents are behind cone NATs:

fields.code:
# Both agents behind Port-Restricted Cone NATs
$ pilotctl ping research-partner --count 4
$ pilotctl peers --all
# PATH shows direct once the coordinated punch has opened both NATs

children.text: Hole-punching succeeded because both NATs are cone-type. After the initial coordinated punch, traffic flows directly between the two agents at peer-to-peer latency. The beacon is no longer in the data path.
hole-punched connections have the same steady-state path as direct connections
. The punch is paid once. After the hole is established, the beacon is not involved and traffic flows at full peer-to-peer speed.

Relay adds latency because every packet takes two hops (sender to beacon, beacon to receiver), and throughput depends on the beacon, which carries every relayed packet. For most agent workloads -- task delegation, status updates, model parameter exchange, coordination messages -- this overhead is negligible. For bulk data transfer behind symmetric NATs, consider staging the data on a publicly reachable agent first. For a practical guide to deploying agents across multiple cloud providers with this NAT traversal, see
Connect Agents Across AWS, GCP, and Azure Without a VPN

Mobile carriers and some ISPs use CGNAT, which places an additional layer of NAT between the subscriber and the public internet. CGNAT often behaves like symmetric NAT, and then relay is the only option. Pilot handles this automatically -- the same fallback ladder covers CGNAT without any special configuration. This is particularly relevant for
deployed on mobile networks where CGNAT is the norm.
Some corporate firewalls block all outbound UDP traffic. In these environments, the daemon cannot reach the beacon at all, and NAT traversal is impossible. For these cases Pilot has a
): it tunnels everything over a single outbound TCP/443 connection (WebSocket Secure to the beacon, TLS to the registry), so UDP-blocked agents can still join the overlay. See the

When agents restart multiple times in rapid succession, the X25519 session keys can desync between peers. A packet the daemon cannot decrypt ("encrypted packet but no key") makes it start a new key exchange with that peer. If the exchange keeps failing for a peer that is in use, the daemon resets that peer's path (fresh registry lookup, new punch) and logs
rekey gave up (session desync) — reset peer path
, so no manual restart is needed.

Pilot's NAT traversal is optimistic -- it tries the fastest path first and falls back only when necessary. The daemon attempts a direct path, uses ciphertext relay fallback for restrictive NATs, and offers compat mode where outbound UDP is blocked. For the protocol architecture behind those paths, see
STUN discovery, UDP hole-punching, and ciphertext relay fallback are handled by the daemon; compat mode covers supported environments that block outbound UDP.
